what_its_for: Laronidase is used to treat a rare genetic disease called Mucopolysaccharidosis I (MPS I), also known as Hurler, Hurler-Scheie, or Scheie syndrome. In MPS I, your body is missing an important enzyme that breaks down certain sugars. Without this enzyme, these sugars build up in your body and cause damage to your organs, bones, and other tissues. Laronidase replaces the missing enzyme to help reduce this buildup and improve your symptoms.
how_to_take: Laronidase is NOT a pill or injection you give yourself at home. It is given by a healthcare provider as a slow drip through a vein (called an IV infusion). Each infusion session usually takes about 3 to 4 hours. You will receive this treatment at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. Before your infusion, your doctor or nurse may give you antihistamines or other medicines to help prevent allergic reactions. Always tell your care team how you are feeling during and after the infusion.
dosing: The usual dose is 0.58 mg for every kilogram (kg) of your body weight, given once a week. Your doctor will calculate the exact amount based on your weight. Do not try to adjust your dose on your own. Your healthcare team will prepare and give you the correct amount each time.
missed_dose: Since your infusions are given by a healthcare provider, it is important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you have to miss an infusion for any reason, contact your doctor or infusion center right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Missing doses may reduce how well the medicine works, so try not to skip any sessions.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. Your infusion center or pharmacy handles the storage. For your information: the medicine must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should NOT be frozen. Once the infusion is prepared, it must be used right away or within a specific short time frame. Do not shake the vials.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you notice any of the following during or after your infusion: difficulty breathing, wheezing, or shortness of breath; chest tightness or pain; severe rash, hives, or skin flushing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; rapid or irregular heartbeat; dizziness or fainting; nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain; fever or chills; severe headache. Also let your doctor know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as well as if you start any new medications.
what_to_avoid: Avoid missing your weekly infusion appointments, as regular treatment is very important for this medicine to work well. Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some may interact with laronidase. Avoid receiving live vaccines without checking with your doctor first.
when_it_works: Laronidase does not cure MPS I, but it helps manage the disease by replacing the missing enzyme. Some people notice improvements in breathing, walking ability, and energy levels within weeks to months of starting treatment. However, results can vary from person to person. It is very important to continue treatment even if you feel better, because stopping may cause symptoms to return or worsen. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular check-ups and tests.
special_populations: Children: Laronidase is approved for use in children, including infants, and is dosed based on body weight. Parents or caregivers should discuss any concerns with the child's doctor. Elderly patients: There is limited information on use in older adults. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits will need to be carefully discussed. Kidney or liver disease: Let your doctor know if you have any kidney or liver problems, as this may affect your care. A patient registry (MPS I Registry) exists to collect long-term safety and effectiveness information — ask your doctor if you would like to enroll.
